title: Gifting QSBS Shares: A Strategic Opportunity That Requires Careful Planning
summary: Learn how gifting QSBS shares may help transfer wealth, reduce estate tax exposure, and preserve potential Section 1202 benefits through careful planning.
body_markdown:
For founders, investors, and business owners holding[Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS)](https://www.cbiz.com/services/tax/business-tax/qualified-small-business-stock) , gifting shares can be a valuable estate and tax planning strategy. When executed thoughtfully, a gift of QSBS may help transfer future appreciation to family members or trusts while potentially extending QSBS benefits to the recipient that might not be available to the donor. However, the timing of the gift, applicable gift tax rules, and evolving IRS scrutiny of this planning technique all warrant careful consideration.


## Why Gifting QSBS Can Be Attractive


Under Internal Revenue Code Section 1202, eligible shareholders may exclude a significant amount of gain when QSBS is sold, provided all requirements are satisfied. Because QSBS generally retains its status when transferred by gift, recipients may be able to benefit from the donor’s holding period and preserve access to the potential gain exclusion. And the gain exclusion amount for recipients might be in excess of the amount available to the donor (see “Stacking Strategies,” below). This creates planning opportunities for shareholders seeking to transfer wealth while reducing future estate tax exposure.


For[middle-market business](https://www.cbiz.com/insights/mid-market-pulse) owners anticipating a sale or liquidity event, gifting QSBS before the event can shift future appreciation out of their taxable estate while allowing family members or certain trusts to participate in potential tax benefits associated with the stock.


## Timing Matters


The timing of a QSBS gift can significantly affect the overall tax outcome.


In general, business owners considering a gift should evaluate making it well in advance of a planned sale or other liquidity event. A gift made before a company’s value increases substantially may reduce the amount of the owner’s lifetime gift and estate tax exemption that is consumed. Earlier planning can also allow time to address valuation considerations and trust structuring issues.


Timing is also important because QSBS eligibility is closely tied to holding-period requirements. While a donee generally receives the donor’s holding period, proper documentation and planning remain critical to preserving potential benefits. Additionally, shareholders should consider how pending transactions, letters of intent and other pre-sale activities may affect the effectiveness of a gifting strategy.


## Gift Tax Exclusions and Other Considerations


Although a gift of QSBS may offer compelling income tax and estate planning opportunities, it does not eliminate gift tax considerations.


Annual gift tax exclusions may allow donors to transfer a small portion of value each year without using lifetime exemption amounts, depending on the structure of the transfer and the recipient. Gifts exceeding applicable exclusion amounts generally reduce the donor’s remaining lifetime gift and estate tax exemption. Business owners should work closely with their tax advisors to determine the reporting requirements and long-term impact of a planned transfer.


Valuation is another important consideration. Because QSBS often involves interests in privately held companies, supporting the value reported on a gift tax return may require a qualified appraisal or valuation analysis. Proper documentation can become especially important if the IRS later reviews the transaction.


## Carryover Basis Implications


Recipients of gifted QSBS generally receive a carryover basis. In other words, the donee typically assumes the donor’s tax basis in the stock rather than receiving a step-up in basis at the time of the gift.


A consequence of carryover basis means that when the recipient later seeks to claim QSBS gain exclusion benefits, the transferred shares continue to trace back to the donor’s original cost basis. This often prevents the donee from getting enhanced gain exclusion potentials, since the 10-times-basis calculation will reference the donor’s original cost basis figure, which is often lower than the stock’s fair market value on the gifting date. At the same time, donees should understand that any built-in gain existing at the time of the gift generally transfers with the stock. As a result, basis tracking and recordkeeping remain essential throughout the ownership period.


## Stacking Strategies and Expected IRS Guidance


One of the most discussed QSBS planning techniques involves “stacking.” Because the section 1202 gain exclusion is applied on a per-taxpayer basis, some taxpayers have used gifts to family members, trusts or other planning structures to multiply available QSBS exclusions. Current law expressly recognizes that QSBS status and holding periods extend to transfers by gift. For example, a gift of QSBS generally creates multiple instances of the donor’s single $10 million or $15 million gain exclusion amount, since the full gain exclusion amount is available on a per-taxpayer basis. This multiplication (stacking) will increase the cumulative gain exclusion potential between each shareholder, who often belong to the same family.


However, the IRS and Treasury Department have recently signaled concerns regarding QSBS stacking strategies. According to recent comments from Treasury officials, guidance is under development that could limit or restrict certain stacking arrangements. Taxpayers considering these strategies should recognize that future guidance may significantly affect planning opportunities and could potentially take an aggressive view toward transactions the government considers abusive.


## Planning Ahead


Gifting QSBS can be a powerful tool for transferring wealth, reducing future estate exposure, and potentially enhancing valuable tax benefits. Yet the strategy’s success depends on thoughtful execution, careful timing, and an understanding of both gift tax and income tax consequences.


Given the evolving regulatory environment surrounding QSBS stacking techniques, business owners should evaluate gifting opportunities sooner rather than later and consult their tax advisors to determine whether a transfer aligns with their broader wealth and succession planning goals.

**What Is QSBS?**


QSBS refers to shares in certain C corporations that qualify for significant tax advantages upon sale or exchange, if specific requirements are met. In many cases, eligible shareholders can exclude a substantial portion, or potentially up to 100%, of capital gains from federal tax, subject to statutory limits and holding period rules.


**Who May Qualify**


QSBS eligibility generally depends on factors such as the type of business, asset thresholds, stock issuance conditions, and holding period requirements. Founders, early investors, and certain key stakeholders in qualifying C corporations are most often in a position to benefit.

#### Frequently Asked Questions


Generally, yes. QSBS can retain its status when transferred by gift, allowing the recipient to potentially benefit from the donor’s holding period and preserve access to available Section 1202 gain exclusion benefits, provided all applicable requirements continue to be met.


Timing can significantly affect both estate and gift tax outcomes. Making a gift before a substantial increase in company value may reduce the amount of lifetime gift and estate tax exemption used and provide additional time to address valuation, documentation, and trust planning considerations.


A gift of QSBS does not eliminate gift tax considerations. Annual gift tax exclusions may apply in some circumstances, while larger transfers can reduce a donor’s remaining lifetime gift and estate tax exemption. Reporting requirements may also apply.


Recipients of gifted QSBS generally receive a carryover basis, meaning they assume the donor’s tax basis in the shares. Because built-in gain typically transfers with the stock, maintaining accurate basis records is important for future tax reporting and planning.


QSBS stacking refers to strategies that use gifts to family members, trusts, or other structures to increase the number of taxpayers eligible for Section 1202 gain exclusions. While current law permits certain transfers of QSBS, the IRS, and Treasury Department have indicated that guidance may be forthcoming that could limit some stacking arrangements.
